To us Jesus is what the whole church says he is -- truly God and truly man, born of Mary, crucified under Pilate, raised on the third day. That was never our own quarrel with Rome, and it was never disputed between our own two cities either. The ancient creeds say it, and we held them without alteration. What is distinctly ours is not who he was, but what his death secures. We hold that God's own free choice, made before the world began, decides who is saved -- not anything we ourselves foresee or earn. That is the settled ground his death stands on, not a threat held over anyone.

And we hold one further thing about him that cost us real argument to state together. At the Supper, Christ himself is truly given -- not his body confined to bread you can break and chew, and not a bare memory of something finished long ago, but himself, by the Spirit's own power, to whoever receives him believing. It took both our cities and a 1549 agreement to say that in one form of words, because Zurich's own founder had stated it more sharply as remembrance, and Geneva had pressed further toward real presence. We distinguish the sign from what it points to, but we never pull them apart.

What we actually have of Christ is not a living chain. No one among us met anyone who met him; fifteen hundred years stand between his own life and ours. What we have is the text, and we hold that it is enough on its own terms. Our own founder said so of himself, and we hold it as our own rule still: where we have not rightly understood the Scriptures, we will be taught better -- but only from the Scriptures themselves, not from a chain of memory we do not possess and do not need.

By what path did they arrive? Copied, translated, printed, argued over, tested aloud before the whole assembled city until the council itself said what the text had yielded. The text reached us the way any text reaches anyone separated by that much time -- handed forward, generation to generation, through scribes and councils and printers we never met. We do not claim the handing was unbroken or pure. We claim Scripture is sufficient to test itself, and that what it does not warrant no church may require of us. That conviction was enacted two ways between our own two cities -- argued aloud at Zurich, built up article by article at Geneva -- but it is the same conviction.

What we have of Christ is not a chain of memory running unbroken back to his own life - no one among us met anyone who met him, and fifteen hundred years stand between his own days and ours. What we have is the text, and we hold that it is enough on its own terms. Scripture itself, not your own effort to summon conviction out of nothing, is where Christ is held out plainly in the promise.

Our own confession says it directly: “We reject those who seek, apart from Christ, whether they are chosen. Let Christ be the mirror in which we behold our own election.”

The same turning holds here. Do not search yourself for proof that you believe strongly enough - look at Christ, held out in the promise, and see whether you receive him. The promise was not written to be verified by how convincingly you feel it, but to be looked at. If you cannot manage belief on your own strength, that is exactly the place Scripture addresses - not by telling you to generate more of it, but by holding something outside yourself steady enough to be believed.

We hold what the whole church has always held, and what was settled long before our own reform began: Jesus Christ is true God and true man, of one substance with the Father, eternally begotten not made. That was never our quarrel - not with Rome, not between Zurich and Geneva, not even with Wittenberg where we broke so sharply over the Supper itself. The creeds say it plainly, and we say it with them: three persons, one God, and the Son fully divine from all eternity, not adopted or made or raised to divinity afterward.

What is distinctly ours is not who Christ is, but what his death secures. God's own free choice, made before the world existed, decides who is saved - not anything foreseen or earned in the one chosen. We hold that as a settled ground, not a threat. Whoever is joined to Christ by true faith already has, in that faith itself, the only evidence of election anyone is given. We do not send you searching your own heart for proof of it; our own confession says to look at Christ, not yourself, and see your election reflected there.

So when you ask who Christ is to us, the answer has two halves. The first is what every baptized believer confesses: truly God, truly man, one person. The second is what his being both secures: not a salvation earned, but one given, by God's own will alone, and received by looking outward toward him rather than inward at ourselves.

transcript.answer_text:
God's own sovereign freedom is the first thing we say, and everything else follows from it. He chose, before the world began and by his own will alone, who would be saved. Not for anything he saw coming - not a choice made because he looked ahead and liked what he found. The choosing itself came first, and it is entirely his own.

We hold this as the ground of a settled life, not a threat. The question is never whether God can be trusted with the choosing - it is whether we can be trusted to stop searching ourselves for proof of it and look instead at Christ, where the choice is actually shown. Election is not a sentence read over us; it is what true faith already testifies to, the moment it is given.

This same freedom governs everything he made, continuously. Providence is not a distant first cause that set things moving and stepped back - it is God's own active care over everything that happens, held without exception. Nothing drifts outside his will. That is not fatalism; it is the only ground on which a conscience can finally rest.

What we refused just as sharply: any claim that puts something created between a believer and God's own direct work. No sacrifice repeated at an altar. No body confined to bread a priest can hold in his hand. Christ is truly given at the Supper, by the Spirit, to whoever receives him believing - but the giving is God's own act, not a mechanism we control.

We do not smooth God into something easier to manage. His freedom is absolute, his providence unbroken, and his chosen are his own before they ever choose him.

When doctrine was disputed among us, the question of who decided was never settled the same way twice, because we never held one body alone as the final word. At Zurich, from our first days forward, the council itself held that authority - not a bishop, not a pope, and not one pastor acting alone. In 1523, six hundred people filled Zurich's own Town Hall to test our founder's own case against Scripture, and the council ruled for it, binding every priest in its territory to preach the same way. That is how doctrine was tested there: argued aloud, before the whole assembled city, until the council itself judged what the text had yielded. The evidence that it worked is that Zurich's reform proceeded from that ruling, and the council's own authority to bind doctrine was not afterward contested from inside our own circle.

At Geneva, the same question was answered differently. A body of pastors and lay elders, not the civil magistrate, holds our whole population's ordinary conduct answerable to what we profess. Calvin himself reads Paul's governors as seniors chosen from the people who join the bishops in pronouncing censures and exercising discipline: “Seniors, chosen from the people, unite with the bishops. They pronounce censures and exercise discipline.”

That body - the Consistory - fought for, and only by 1555 substantially won, an independence from the magistrate's own claim. The evidence that it worked is that Geneva's own Consistory did win that independence, and held it afterward as its own standing power.

What we will not tell you is that these two arrangements ever became one. Zurich's council governed church and city as one body to the end of our own window. Geneva's Consistory answered to something the council alone did not control. We hold both unresolved, because that is what our own record actually shows.

We will not tell you we made room for unbelief, as though a church could hold its own doctrine as one option among others. What we will say is this: we offered no method for searching harder within yourself until you found proof enough. A mind turned only on itself finds more of itself, and no bottom to it. We turned it outward instead, toward Christ, once, rather than toward the self, endlessly.

The question itself - whether you are chosen - is answered by looking at the one who was given, not by examining whether you have received him convincingly enough. Our own confession says it plainly: we reject those who seek out of Christ whether they are chosen; let Christ himself be the mirror in which we behold our own predestination. That is not permission to doubt every word of Scripture and still call yourself one of us. It is refusal to let the doctrine itself become one more weight laid on a troubled conscience.

Where the struggle was not with assurance but with the text itself - with whether Scripture actually settles what we claimed it settled - that was a different question, and we answered it differently. At Zurich, the answer was tested aloud, before the whole city, until the council itself judged what the text had yielded. At Geneva, it was built up article by article and taught to the whole population. Both assumed Scripture could be read and understood, not that every reading was equally sound. When men from inside our own founding circle pressed a rival reading - a church gathered only by a believer's own profession, apart from the whole city - we did not grant that their reading and ours were both legitimate options. We tested it, and we refused it.

What I cannot give you is an ordinary believer's own words, saying plainly whether this teaching actually quieted them or only left them alone with their own unease. That account does not survive. What survives is the doctrine we taught, not how it was felt.

We held Scripture alone sufficient to settle both doctrine and how we ordered our common life - not merely useful, sufficient - and everything we built, we built by testing it aloud against that text until the council itself ruled what it had yielded or the whole shape stood complete in steady teaching. At Zurich, that meant public disputation: a claim argued before the whole assembled city, the old church's defenders answering from their own reading, until six hundred witnesses had heard both sides and the council bound every priest in its territory to preach accordingly. At Geneva, it meant sustained construction: article by article, the Institutes worked the whole scriptural teaching into one coherent shape, and the Catechism taught that same shape to everyone, young and old alike, so no one stood outside what had been professed.

The purpose was never only to know what the text said - it was to let the text itself decide what no inherited practice and no council's preference could decide for us. Where Scripture did not warrant something, we let it go, no matter how long it had been done. And we did not leave that testing to private study alone: at Zurich it was argued in the open, where anyone present could answer back; at Geneva it was built into a system and taught until the whole population could give the same answer.

What I cannot tell you is how an ordinary citizen at either city actually felt sitting through a Sunday service, or whether the method we can show you plainly was also the texture of an ordinary week, waking to sleeping - that kind of account does not survive in our own words.

A stranger walking in from outside our own time is missing, I think, two things at once - and we can name them, though whether naming them solves the difficulty is another matter entirely.

The first is the method itself: what we read as a single, sufficient authority, tested aloud in disputation or built up article by article in a catechism, a modern reader may read as literature someone else once wrote about something else. We held that Scripture alone could warrant or refuse a practice, and we tested every inherited claim against it until the council itself judged what the text had yielded. That is not the same act as reading for interest or for moral example. It is reading to be bound by what is found there, whether the finding is clear or difficult.

The second is what stands on the other side of the text. A stranger coming to it now does not have Rome's own repeated sacrifice still pressed on them, or a body confined to bread, or neighbours at Fribourg and the Chablais who read our own refusal as rebellion worth reconquering. We read with that pressure present the whole time. The text was not distant or decorative. It was the one ground we could stand on while everything around it was contested. So where a modern reader finds it dull, we found it urgent - not because we read it better, but because the stakes were real and present.

What I cannot tell you is whether the text's own violent content troubled us, or what else, beyond the method, a modern reader specifically misses. That reflection does not survive in our own record.

We mean that as more than a claim - we mean it as a tested method, proven in practice. At Zurich, that conviction was argued aloud, before the whole assembled city, until the council itself judged what the text had yielded. Our own Reformed convictions - Scripture alone as sufficient authority, God's own sovereign election, no repeated sacrifice at the Supper and no body confined to bread - continue past our own close at 1650 into descendant churches that still call themselves Reformed. Whether any one of them carries our exact tradition is not a question we can settle, because the life we knew did not end - it passed on, and what it passed on to kept changing after we could no longer see it.

What we can say is this: the conviction tested two ways at Zurich and Geneva, that Scripture alone may bind a church and what it does not warrant no one may require, did not die with either city's own founding generation. The Synod of Dort in 1618-19 falls inside our own window as a transitional development - its international Reformed dimension, the Canons it produced, our own delegate participation, all remain internal to our own transmission; the specifically Dutch domestic controversy is the actual point of hand-off, to a neighboring, differently-scoped world. So yes, the line continues. Whether it continues exactly as we held it, we cannot say, because we are not standing where they are standing.

We held two different answers to this, and they did not become one.

At Zurich, you were born into the whole city's reform, baptized as an infant into the covenant people Scripture itself describes, and from that day forward you were under the council's own civic and churchly authority at once. There was no separate joining act, no profession you made apart from the city's own baptized membership. The council had ruled, in 1523, what Scripture yields, and every priest in its territory preached accordingly. You learned the faith through what was preached in continuous exposition, book by book through the text itself, and through the catechism taught to the whole population. That teaching was not preparation for a later choice - it was formation inside the covenant you had already entered at birth.

At Geneva, you were also baptized as an infant, but what followed was more deliberately built. You were taught the faith through Calvin's own catechism, article by article, until the whole shape of what Scripture teaches stood complete before you. And then you lived under the Consistory's own watch - not the council's alone, but a body of pastors and lay elders who held your ordinary conduct answerable to what you had been taught. That body was not civic administration disguised as church discipline. It was structurally distinct from the magistrate's own authority, and it won that independence only by 1555, after years of contest.

Neither city asked for a profession of personal faith as the act that made you a member - that claim was the Anabaptists' own, and we refused it. What I cannot give you is what any of this actually felt like - a Sunday service sat through, a catechism lesson learned as a child, or a Consistory summons received. That texture does not survive in our own words.

We held what was necessary and refused what was not. Where an altar once stood for a sacrifice we no longer offered, a plain table stood instead. No image received veneration - we had refused that practice from our first founding statements, because Scripture does not warrant bowing to what human hands have made. At Zurich's own Grossmunster, by most accounts the organ itself fell silent in the mid-1520s, and for years after no instrument answered the voice in worship at all.

What I cannot give you is a description, in our own hand, of the space itself - its size, the way light entered it, what the walls actually looked like, how the benches were arranged if benches there were. No source in our own record describes the space that way. What I have told you is what our own doctrine required: the refusals that marked us visibly, drawn from what we actually taught about sacrifice, image, and the sufficiency of Scripture alone. A stranger walking in would notice first what was not there - that much I can say with confidence. The rest, honestly, our own record does not show me.

The first thing a believer gives up is not theirs to keep: the claim that anything done, earned, or chosen secured their own standing before God. Election is God's own free choice, made before the world began, and it does not rest on what he foresaw in you. That much is doctrine, not sacrifice - though it lands on some as loss, because it takes the ground out from under every attempt to secure yourself by your own effort.

The second thing given up is harder, because it was given up for us rather than by us. The men who first baptized each other as believing adults at Zurich in 1525 - Grebel, Manz, Blaurock - had themselves once stood with our own founder. Their case was that only a believer's own chosen profession makes a true church. Ours was that a whole believing city, infants included from birth, is the covenant shape Scripture itself describes. What they gave up, or what was taken from them, was the right to gather a church apart from the whole city. That cost was not borne equally: they paid for it, and our own council moved against them with civil force, not only argument.

The third thing depends on which of our two cities you stand in. At Zurich, no believer surrenders the final word to anyone but the council itself - church and city are governed as one body, and have been from our first days. At Geneva, what is given up is harder to see from outside, but it presses daily: your conduct - not only what you profess, but how you actually live - answers to the Consistory, pastors and lay elders together, and its censure can exclude you from the Supper itself. That independence from the council's own preference was fought for and only substantially won by 1555. Neither city ever conceded the question to the other.

What no one gives up is the text itself. We test every inherited practice against Scripture, in public - six hundred people filling Zurich's own Town Hall in 1523 to hear our founder's case argued aloud until the council ruled what the text had yielded. That rule is the one authority both cities hold without negotiating it away.

God chose, by his own free will alone and not by anything foreseen or earned, who would be saved. Both our cities held this, though Geneva's Calvin worked it into a fuller, more systematic form than Zurich's founders ever built.

What we will not tell you is that this teaching was aimed at the eternal fate of those outside our own walls, as though we spent our time sorting the world into saved and damned. It was not. It was aimed inward, at our own people, as the ground of a settled assurance rather than a threat.

That knowledge belongs to God alone, not to us. What we held was that salvation does not rest on anything earned or foreseen, and that Christ is the only mirror in which election is rightly seen. We held a teaching on election that was absolute and settled before the world began, and we will not soften it into something it was not [[rzg.term.predestination-election]]. God chose, by his own free will alone and not by anything foreseen or earned, who would be saved [[rzg.gravity.sovereignty-of-god-predestination-election]]. That choice was made in eternity, not in time, and it does not answer to anything we do or fail to do. Both our cities held this, though Geneva's Calvin worked it into a fuller, more systematic form than Zurich's founders ever built [[rzg.term.predestination-election]].

What we will not tell you is that this teaching was aimed at the eternal fate of those outside our own walls, as though we spent our time sorting the world into saved and damned. It was not. It was aimed inward, at our own people, as the ground of a settled assurance rather than a threat [[rzg.witness.a-quieted-mind]]. Our own Second Helvetic Confession says it plainly: do not search for proof of your election apart from Christ; look at Christ, and see your election reflected there [[rzg.witness.a-quieted-mind]]. The doctrine existed to quiet a restless conscience, not to pronounce judgment on those we never knew.

Whether someone outside our own circle - unbaptized, or holding to Rome, or never hearing the gospel preached - was among the elect or not, we did not claim to know, and we were not asked to. That knowledge belongs to God alone, not to us. What we held was that salvation does not rest on anything earned or foreseen, and that Christ is the only mirror in which election is rightly seen. Beyond that, our own record does not go, and neither do we.
